PETRO-CANADA PROPOSED TAKEOVER OF SUNCOR INC.-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Whereas in a New York address the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) indicated that Suncor Incorporated is targeted for takeover by the Canadian government through Petro-Canada, and whereas this explains why the same minister is offering Suncor Incorporated $16.75 a barrel as against $38 a barrel which is being offered to other companies in the same area for the same quality of crude oil, 1 therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling):
That this House, in deploring this violation of security laws and this tricky, underhanded, under-the-table, unscrupulous method of devaluating the shares of Suncor in preparation for the kill, urges the Prime Minister to prepare a scroll in honour of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources as being, next to he himself, the trickiest and most outstanding under-the-table and unscrupulous manipulator in the Liberal cabinet.

GARRISON DIVERSION
subsubtopic: ON-SITE MONITORING OF PROJECT-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that the secretary of the interior of the United States has apportioned an additional $3 million for the Garrison diversion unit in North Dakota, that moneys are still being allocated for further construction of this project and that it is well known that the completion of the Garrison diversion will cause irreparable damage to Canadian waters, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie).
That this government have on-site monitoring as the construction proceeds and that our consular staff in Washington monitor the appropriate committees of the U.S. Congress and report findings to this House on a regular basis so that we may be kept up to date on the status of this project.

subsubtopic: CONDITIONS OF INDIAN COMMUNITIES IN NORTHERN MANITOBA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of a report prepared for the federal government which indicates that Indian reserves in northern Manitoba have inadequate garbage and sewage disposal, which is contaminating drinking water supplies and causing a high rate of hepatitis and dysentery among northern Indians, and in view of the knowledge of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development of this problem for years, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy):
That this House instructs the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to table the report prepared for Environment Canada and turned over to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of National Health and Welfare, to provide a statement on motions concerning the reasons why the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has failed to act on the deplorable health hazards cited in this report and to outline the steps he proposes to adopt to eliminate this inexcusable and intolerable health threat faced by northern Manitoban Indian communities.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Inflation, unemployment, high mortgage interest rates and, in some cases, a total lack of accommodation are severely limiting the ability of Canadians to obtain adequate housing, especially those on low or fixed incomes. Since the Liberal government has abandoned these Canadians in every area of housing policy, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko):
That this House direct the government to rectify its inaction and lack of policy in the housing field and implement a shelter allowance program for Canadian families.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION
subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE-INQUIRY WHETHER REPORTING DEADLINE WILL BE EXTENDED
speechtext:
From the evidence given up to now by the various witnesses, it is obvious that all of them are in favour of enshrining a charter of rights in the constitution. However, some would want us to go further. That is why, in view of the representations made, I say again to the Leader of the NDP that I am quite ready to discuss this with the House leaders. I think that is the proper procedure under the circumstances, namely a possible extension of the deadline. Last week, the hon. member asked for a two-week extension. I say to him again today that we are prepared to discuss the matter. However, the Leader of the New Democratic Party must realize that I made this offer in early October, after the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition complained in his speech about the December 9 deadline, and also after the Tory House leader wrote me a letter in which he took exception to the fact that at the third stage we would be discussing a committee report rather than the resolution itself. At that time, that is in the first week or ten days of October, I made it clear to my fellow House leaders that I was prepared to discuss the committee deadline and also the possibility that we consider the resolution itself rather than a motion for concurrence in the committee report. However, I required a reasonable indication as to the total length of the debate and also as to the procedure to be followed for the consideration of amendments at the third stage.
The Leader of the NDP no doubt realizes that without a set procedure for moving amendments at this third stage, it could become a real hodge podge. After three weeks of debate, we might find ourselves still on a subamendment to clause 3 of the resolution which contains 57 altogether. Therefore, all I ask is that the opposition parties be reasonable, and especially that they agree to negotiate. Again, last week, I repeated this offer. I must recognize that some of the parliamentary leaders were very receptive to this idea, and I certainly hope that in the days ahead all of them will agree to plan sensibly the remainder of the debate, both at the committee stage and on third reading.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION
subsubtopic: SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE-INQUIRY WHETHER REPORTING DEADLINE WILL BE EXTENDED

Madam Speaker, it is important that this point is very clear. Nobody is proposing a filibuster on this particular measure. What is being suggested, I believe reasonably, by members on this side of the House and by some members on the other side of the House is that there be adequate time, both in committee and after the committee reports, to discuss important amendments to our constitution. What I would like clear from the government House leader is that he is not considering a trade-off. Is the government House leader suggesting to the House that there will be a time extension for the committee to do its important work, but that the government is considering reducing the amount of time the House would reasonably require for it to do justice to the matter?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROCEDURE GOVERNING PARTICIPATION IN HOUSE COMMITTEE MEETINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a brief question of privilege or point of order to raise with respect to the practices of this House and its committees. I was not at the committee meeting or other meetings involved personally where this has been taking place, but there is a growing practice of refusing members of Parliament, who are not specifically named on the lists of members forming standing committees, participation in the deliberations of the committees. That happened to the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) yesterday in the Standing Committee on Transport, I believe. He was accomodated by the chief government whip, who simply deleted his own name and substituted the name of the hon. member for Peterborough therefor. However, the committee chairman and the clerk seemed to be of the view that members who are not specifically named on the roster of members forming that standing committee were not entitled to participate in the deliberations of that standing committee.
It has long been the practice here, for many, many years, that notwithstanding the fact that the name of a member of Parliament may not be included on the roster of members forming a specific standing committee, he has the inherent right, as indeed is the right of all members, to participate in that committee's deliberations. Normally the practice has been that those members whose names are on the roster of a standing committee are called upon by the chairman first, either to ask questions or to state their views, but subsequent to that any other member who may not be on the roster, if he expresses a desire to do so, is then invited to participate in those deliberations.

I merely raise this at this time so that perhaps the knowledge might be disseminated to the various chairmen of the standing committees that they should not be depriving the rights which are enjoyed by all members of Parliament to participate in committee deliberations, notwithstanding the fact that they are not specifically named on the rosters of standing committees.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROCEDURE GOVERNING PARTICIPATION IN HOUSE COMMITTEE MEETINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have two things to say. First of all, it is true that members of the House, even if their names are not on the roster of a standing committee, may attend the meetings of that committee, but it is up to the chairman to recognize those who take part in the proceedings, and each committee is master of its own procedure. I know that those whose names do not appear on the roster of a committee do not have the right to vote. According to our practice, they are generally entitled to take part in the proceedings if the committee and the chairman agree. However, the hon. member has raised a specific question concerning the Standing Committee on Transport. In the absence of a report from this committee I believe, Madam Speaker, that it would be very difficult for Your Honour to rule on what may have happened. This committee is master of its own procedure, and I believe that it would be improper for you to make a ruling without having a report from that committee.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROCEDURE GOVERNING PARTICIPATION IN HOUSE COMMITTEE MEETINGS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am very happy with the first part of the response of the government House leader because in those remarks he confirmed my view of the past practice of the House that members who are not named on the rosters of particular standing committees have the right to participate if called upon by chairmen to do so.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROCEDURE GOVERNING PARTICIPATION IN HOUSE COMMITTEE MEETINGS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in support of the position taken by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), may I point out to him that he does not have to rely on what he says is past practice. The matter is covered in the rules. There was a time years ago when it was a matter of practice, but a few years ago the rules were amended.
Standing Order 65(9) says quite clearly:
Any member of the House who is not a member of a standing or special committee, may, unless the House or the committee concerned otherwise orders, take part in the public proceedings of the committee, but he may not vote or move any motion, nor shall he be part of any quorum.
I suggest, Madam Speaker, that the wording of that Standing Order 65(9) does not leave it to the discretion of the Chair. Unless the committee passes an order saying that non-members of the committee may not speak, the right of such non-members to speak is clearly provided in Standing Order 65(9).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-PROCEDURE GOVERNING PARTICIPATION IN HOUSE COMMITTEE MEETINGS
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for having read to members of the House the Standing Order to which this point of order refers. Although members usually know the Standing Orders very well, it is not a bad idea to read them from time to time. I think the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) will agree that this Standing Order says exactly what has to be said about the committees. His point of order might be considered by the committee itself. The Standing Orders are quite clear that the committees are responsible for their own procedure and that any member who wishes to participate in the proceedings may do so.

GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1969 Metric Commission Order PC 1971-1146 10 June, 1971
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, pursuant to section 18 of the Government Organization Act, 1969, is pleased hereby to make the annexed Order to Establish a Preparatory Commission for Conversion to the Metric System.
AN ORDER TO ESTABLISH A PREPARATORY COMMISSION FOR CONVERSION TO THE METRIC SYSTEM Short Title
1.	This Order may be cited as the Metric Commission Order.
Interpretation
2.	In this Order,
(a)	"Commission" means the Preparatory Commission for
Metric Conversion established pursuant to section 3; and
(b)	"Minister" means the Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce.
Establishment of Commission
3.	A committee is hereby established to be known as the Preparatory Commission for Metric Conversion, consisting of
(a)	a full-time member who shall be the chairman of the
commission, and
(b)	not more than fifteen part-time members, to be appointed by the governor in council.
4.	The commission may make such rules as may be necessary for the conduct of its meetings and the performance of its duties.
5.	(1) The governor in council may, upon the request of the commission, provide the commission with the services of such officers and employees employed by or in any department of the Government of Canada as are necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the commission, and the commission may obtain the advice and assistance of any department or agency of the Government of Canada.
(2) The commission may engage such organizations or persons having a technical or specialized knowledge on any matter relating to the work of the commission to advise and assist the commission in the performance of its duties.
Purposes and Powers
6.	The commission is established for the purpose of advising the minister on plans for conversion to the metric system, and for such purpose, the commission may
(a)	initiate, co-ordinate and undertake investigations, surveys and studies relating to the implications of conversion to the metric system in different sectors of the Canadian economy;
(b)	prepare, in consultation and cooperation with any department or agency of the Government of Canada, any department or agency of the government or any province, the Standards Council of Canada, or other interested parties an overall program for conversion to the metric system which will ensure, as far as possible, that any programs for such conversion in the different sectors of the Canadian economy are phased and co-ordinated in order that
(i)	the benefits of conversion to the metric system are achieved at minimal cost, and
(ii)	conversion to the metric system as a whole is effected to the best advantage to Canada; and
(c)	furnish, publish and disseminate information concerning conversion to the metric system.
7.	The commission shall advise the minister on the need for legislation or any other action that may be required to facilitate conversion to the metric system.
8.	The commission shall make such reports on its activities from time to time as the minister may require.
Oath
9.	Each member of the commission shall, before taking up his duties, take and subscribe an oath or affirmation in the following form:
"I.	solemnly
and sincerely swear (or affirm) that I will faithfully and honestly fulfil the duties that devolve upon me by reason of my appointment as a member of the Preparatory Commission for Metric Conversion and that I will not, without due authority in that behalf, disclose or make known any matter that comes to my knowledge by reason of such appointment. (In the case where an oath is taken add, 'So help me God')".

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise as I did last night to continue debate on Bill C-6 and to make an additional point to the three points I made last night.
Just to review very quickly my three points of last night, first of all they dealt with the location of chartered banks within the nation, or the location of the head offices of chartered banks within the nation. I pointed out that three of them, with a capitalization of $100 million, were located in western Canada; that seven of them, with a capitalization of $700 million, were located in central Canada, that is, four in Montreal and three in Toronto; that only one was located in the Atlantic provinces, in Halifax, with a capitalization of $50 million.
I made the point that serious consideration or an examination should be given by the banking system itself in terms of relocating its head offices in this nation, as big as it is and as dependent upon the banking system as it is. I suggested that it would be appropriate if one located in Calgary, if one considered St. John's, Newfoundland, and if the other one would perhaps consider Quebec City.
I went on to indicate that, because of the geographical size of the nation and the spread of the population across the nation, it was necessary for the banks to give the utmost consideration to placing on their boards of directors Canadians from all over the land, so that there would be regional representation on their boards of directors.
My third point was in connection with the use of Canada's technological might in terms of working on an export basis. Canada has great capability today in technology and in its amassment of engineering talent to work throughout the world in this area, but it must associate itself with the liberalization of the capitalization of some of these projects. I indicated that the chartered banks should look seriously at setting up a comprehensive system in regard to the use of Canadian technology and technological might overseas.
My fourth point deals with the evolution of a quasi-form of government bank. The shortcomings of the banking system for western Canada have caused much apprehension and concern over the years. For example, for the first time in Alberta there was an ability to amass sufficient capital together to deal with capital needs in the west and permit a growth formula, controlled and directed by the west itself instead of by central
Canada. In this regard it was advisable, on the basis of extracting money from resources, to set up vehicles like the Alberta Energy Company and the Alberta Heritage Savings Trust Fund.
I want to speak about the use of these instruments to Canadianize Canada's oil and gas industry. There are two ways of doing this. One way is to use a blunt instrument to nationalize the oil and gas industry and literally take over segments from government funding and from some form of quasi national banking institution. The present government has embarked upon a system not of Canadianizing the oil and gas industry but of nationalizing it. There are some pluses and minuses with respect to this type of procedure or over-all policy.
As a member of the government in Alberta I was associated rather closely with the oil and gas industry. We decided at one point it was necessary to Canadianize some of the oil and gas industry. We arranged a remarkable tool for accomplishing that without disturbing the existing industry in all its dimensions. We set up the Alberta Energy Company, which is 50 per cent owned by the province of Alberta. The other 50 per cent was sold to the citizens of Alberta, who are Canadians in the truest sense of the word. In every possible way Albertans are Canadians, and they intend to remain as such. With the type of tool we arranged it was possible for Albertans, in conjunction with the Alberta government, to move on an equity share basis on new projects in the province of Alberta and therefore specifically and directly to Canadianize some of the growth of this industry. This was done to assist the industry, and it was done in co-operation with it. It created a terrific impetus to the growth and catalyzation of this industry, not only in Alberta but in western Canada.
Last summer when I was a member of the Progressive Conservative caucus committee on energy I wrote a memorandum in which I specifically proposed a national energy bank. That was a memo I wrote a year ago last August. I also indicated in it that in connection with the national energy bank in an effort to Canadianize some of the oil and gas industry in this nation-indeed, much of the energy industry in this nation-and in conjunction with money from the Alberta Heritage Savings Trust Fund this would effect, on a gradual and co-operative basis, a degree of Canadianization of the energy industry. That is an acceptable way of moving forward, by using the financial resources of this nation to Canadianize in a gradual and acceptable way by using shareholders and government capital, if you wish, to increase the Canadian ownership of two vital industries in this nation.
I would like to put forward a comparison of that system, which is partially working so well in Alberta, and the federal government system of providing a quasi form of banking through their Petroleum Compensation Fund in order to buy additional multinational corporations. They wish to buy them in totality, not to buy 20 per cent or 30 per cent of some of these companies, which would effect some reasonable amount
November 19, 1980

of control, and nationalize them. They want to buy them in totality and add them to the corporate public giant called Petro-Canada, thereby increasing the inefficiency of this corporation. We all know that its inefficiency is increasing dramatically compared to the efficiency of some of the well-managed multinationals.
Mr. Speaker, nobody is against Canadianization of the oil and gas industry, or a movement toward the Canadianization of it through banking institutions or quasi banking institutions, through government funds or shareholders. Nobody is against Canadianization of the oil and gas industry in that way. Some of us have difficulty, though, with the proposal of Canadianization through the process of nationalization, which is a blunt weapon. This is an unacceptable weapon, which can be used in such a way that it could dictate policies, reducing the asset value of companies which have done business in Canada for many years. So they are prime targets for takeover at a low share value. Suncor is an excellent example of this. It was a company that pioneered the oil sands. This was a subject discussed rather hotly and heavily in the question period today. It is known that in the oil sands there are approximately 900 billion barrels of oil. About 74 billion barrels are available through surface mining, and 900 billion are available through in situ mining.

Mr. Speaker, when I spoke yesterday about the Bank Act and about banking institutions in Canada I specifically stated that this system, which is vital to the nation, had enormous power in the circulation of wealth, finances, and the creation of credit. Indeed, I said that it had a great effect on the growth of the social structure and the organization of the nation in totality. I also spoke about the banking system and its effects on the growth and health of the industrial sector of this nation. That is a very vital and substantive part of this banking act. It extends from one end of the nation to the other, putting forward the fundamental nature of commerce.

speechtext: What has that to do with nationalization?

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Of course it does because you can raise money in several ways. Mr. Speaker, I do not have too much time left and one could spend a great deal of time on this topic.
I simply want to reiterate that Canadianization of a vital industry like the oil and gas industry could have been done in
Bank Act
such a way that the industry's growth and performance in terms of self-sufficiency would not have been affected to the extent that it was. This is a fundamental point.
The vital project at Cold Lake is the first of its kind dealing with some 900 billion barrels of oil which are in the ground. It was vital this process and this plant go ahead. That is one of the reasons why I wrote to both the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Premier of Alberta last August. I wanted to do whatever was necessary to see that this plan and this process went ahead, because it was a new form of technological development. By the way, that oil in the ground is better than dollars in any bank, but I wanted to see that this resource was developed and commercialized, since this in situ plant was the first such plant.
The point I am trying to make is that the financial institutions of this nation could have been used rather effectively to Canadianize a substantive portion of the oil and gas industry, as is being done in Alberta through the Alberta Energy Company and through investments of the Heritage Savings and Trust Fund in oil sands plants and in other areas. These institutions could have been used in such a way that they would not affect the industry to any great extent. I am honestly saddened, because I have spent so many years dealing with this industry as a minister in the Alberta government, that we have had to use such blunt instruments in relationship to Canadianizing the oil and gas industry, by nationalizing rather then by Canadian investment in the industry.
Those are my remarks, but I hope to have the opportunity again to speak on the use of Canadian capital, whether it be by the government directly or, indeed, by the people through investors and shareholders, or by corporations themselves, in regard to excess capital and Canadianization of the energy industry in Canada, particularly the oil and gas industry.

speechtext:
They pleased the government, but what pleases the public is of a different consequence to this particular government.
I, like the hon. member for Medicine Hat, the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) and the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), appreciate the amendments which affected agriculture because they did so in an important way. I repeat, though, that the proposals were brought in on behalf of the caisses populaires and credit unions and were primarily supported by Quebec members of the government and opposition members when the act was initially submitted. There were some changes on behalf of those members which were very important, and which will make a better financial structure for Canada.
The act was primarily introduced-as I can see when I compare the 1967 act, which was finally passed in 1971, with the performance of the banks-to give the authority to the banks to perform functions which they were able to perform by virtue of the fact that they were not asked to observe the letter of the Bank Act of 1967 by consecutive ministers of finance over that period of time. The act has opened up the fields into which the banks more or less infringe, with the acquiescence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and his officers who are responsible for the administration and supervision of the regulations.
As a result the banks have been expanded to a degree which gives me great concern. I am concerned that we have established for Canada an oligopoly which will control the financial structures of this nation to the point where the Minister of Finance may not be able to control the money supply or inflation, since he may lose control of the M2 and M3 factors which must be considered in the fiscal and monetary policy of this nation. We are creating a structure which is now involved in virtually all fields of finance. The banking institutions can now go into equity, and under certain circumstances can deal with securities. The banks are into the mortgage business, leasing, and all sorts of fields.
I submit that we have created an oligopoly and abandoned the principle that banks were intended to receive deposits and loan money to creditors primarily for individuals and the businessmen of the country. Now we find that banks have the option of putting such money as they may have at hand into

I am concerned about the expansion of opportunities available to banks, Mr. Speaker, because one by one the provinces have been forced into a structure in which they are financing small business and farmers. I think I am correct in presuming that one of the reasons for this is that, after the 1967 structure was created, there were other places for the banks to put their money. If someone is refused a loan by a bank today, he can approach a government structure such as the Farm Credit Corporation, Small Business Development Bank and so on. Federal officials are encouraging this action. This is not the way the banks should operate, Mr. Speaker. The banks and the government should see to it that all businessmen, farmers, fishermen and others who require funds, are looked after by the banking structure of Canada. That is not the case, however.
We have created an oligopoly. I hope that Canada has a healthy fiscal future and I hope that my fears are not realized. I hope the Minister of Finance and his officials will exert the necessary influence to bring banks back to reality.
I should give an example of why I complain about the operation of the rural banks Mr. Speaker. A business friend of mine approached the bank in his community for a loan. As security, he offered assets valued at more than twice the value of the loan. The bank manager looked at his statement, which had been favourable and progressive, and suggested that he add his house as collateral. He owned the house outright, Mr. Speaker. This man had been engaged in a profitable business for ten or 15 years. There was no way he was going to put his house on the line, as this was not considered necessary according to standard banking practice in other areas of Canada. I checked with other members of this House to find out whether it would have been necessary, had he lived in a city, to do the same thing. The answer was no.
In the branch system in a city where there is a multiplicity of perhaps eight to 15 different bank branches, there is competition. In the village and small town structure of this nation there is no competition and there is nothing in this act which will create competition. That is my complaint. Lack of competition denies opportunity to small businessmen in Canada, and there is no mechanism by which the minister can exert any pressure.

I remember in Winnipeg in the early 1960s we attempted to obtain money for the producing provinces. We tried to raise money in the east. We put small packages together and asked U.S. individuals to help us. That was the method by which a lot of the smaller oil companies got going. I realize the majors were here, but they were not doing all of the exploration. In fact it was the small oil companies to a great extent that brought in the competition for the major companies. It was not through the efforts of Canadians. But it was more than that. During the period of the 1960s and 1970s-and I must admit this is my opinion-the Canadian government actually discouraged the investment of funds.
Over the years those of us who have moved into the oil business could see that the Government of Canada was not encouraging people to enter the oil business. Yet, I find it very strange just two months ago I stood here and said that $600 million of Canadian money, sitting in Canadian banks, was going to leave the country for the United States. Little did I know then that that figure would double within a month and a half. Now over $1 billion of Canadian funds is leaving Canadian banks for the United States. These new enterprises will look at the government and ask "has there been a major shift in policy from being supportive of industry to being a socialist government wanting to take over any industry that is vibrant?" I sat here many months ago listening to members opposite from Quebec speak about their problem of separation. I must say that their problem was nothing compared to ours. You cannot turn ours around by standing here in the House of Commons and saying why the west should stay in Canada. There are studies out now by qualified individuals from the University of Calgary which suggest that it would be better for western Canada to separate.

We cannot treat it like the Quebec problem.

Association and to amend other acts in consequence thereof, be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for the purpose of reconsidering clause 2 with respect to the proposed section 222 at page 246 of the said bill.

Every person who, in any language, uses the word "bank", "banker" or "banking", either alone or in combination with other words, or any word or words of import equivalent thereto, to indicate or describe his business in Canada or any part of his business in Canada without being authorized so to do by this or any other act, is guilty of an offence against this act.
Then it goes on to say:
Every person who uses the name of a bank in a prospectus or advertisement for the sale of securities other than those issued by or guaranteed as to principal and interest by Canada or a province, a municipal or school corporation in Canada or a bank, is guilty of an offence against this act; but this subsection does not apply where such use is required by law and is confined to a statement contained in a prospectus that a corporation is the holder of shares of the capital stock or evidences of indebtedness of a bank.
In short, to any lay person who reads section 157 in our existing Bank Act it would appear that one cannot carry on the business of banking in this country unless one is authorized to carry out the banking business under the Bank Act. That was the law of the land for over 100 years, and it is not to be questioned. What I find most strange is that this government, which pretends to wish to Canadianize industry in this country, and in particular the petroleum industry, is, at the same time "foreignizing" the banking industry in our country in direct defiance of the existing Bank Act. Imagine what they have done in spite of the clear lav; of the land as I read it. They have permitted an estimated 80 to 90 foreign banks to set up operations in the country, with assets totalling something like $8 billion at present, notwithstanding section 157 of the existing Bank Act.
Is it not understandable then why people are so cynical about this government and about the coalition of the government opposite and its NDP allies?

Throughout this document, all kinds of similar comments are to be found. The whole thrust of the document is that, in view of foreign ownership, the only way to put it right, to Canadianize the situation, is through some type of nationalization, ownership by the state as opposed to ownership by the private sector of petroleum companies which are declared to be foreign.
The point I want to make is that, whether or not you believe there is undue foreign ownership in the petroleum industry, surely it is strange to have a government which says, on the one hand, it wants to Canadianize the petroleum industry through state ownership, and at the same time says about the banking industry, which has been one of the truly Canadian owned industries in the country, "We want to open it up so that foreigners can now participate". Not only is the government eager to do it by having Parliament pass the bill which is now before us but, as hon. members will recall and as I have stated, it turns a blind eye to some 80 foreign banks setting up shop here and being active to the tune of $8 billion. In spite of that, the government asks us to believe that somehow or other it is the great Canadian champion.
I sometimes wonder where that illustrious Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) was when all this was going on, that minister who likes to say how much he hopes he will be able to Canadianize industry in this country and ensure it is owned by Canadians to a greater extent. The truth is that the government opposite is hypocritical. We have a government in power which is vacillating, pragmatic, deceitful. Ministers know how to win elections by deceit but, unfortunately, they fail to recognize that you cannot run a country by deceit only.
I suggest that hon. members look through the list of foreign banking corporations which the government has permitted to enter the country. It is truly astounding, notwithstanding the provisions to which I have referred in the existing Bank Act. For example, the Bank of America, which has an office in the Royal Bank Plaza in Toronto, shows assets in Canada amounting to $301 million. Indeed, I raised the subject. I have worked with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for many years and I am prepared, on the basis of my experience, to accept his version of what happened. If others do not wish to accept that version, that is their business.
We heard a great deal from the hon. member for York-Peel about the so-called coalition between the members of the Liberal party and the members of the New Democratic Party. We will see in a very few minutes where the real coalition lies, because members of our party have said on every occasion in the House, and in committee, that they disagree fundamentally with many of the important clauses in the Bank Act and will vote against the act. The hon. members for York-Peel, Calgary North (Mr. Wright), and Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), this afternoon criticized important sections of the act and pointed out what was wrong with them, but when the debate is over in less than one hour, those three supporters of free enterprise, who are so opposed to the so-called socialists on the Liberal side, will vote with those so-called socialists for the exact bill which we will vote against.
I ask the hon. member for York-Peel: who is coalescing with whom? The hon. member for York-Peel says that by moving the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae), we are filibustering the bill. We moved that amendment because we are concerned about the tremendous amount of money involved in the foreign loans which the banks have made. We are particularly concerned about the loans which have been made to countries such as South Africa and Chile. These countries have received loans from such Canadian banks as the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, the Royal Bank, and the Orion Bank in England. Our concerns are shared by such organizations as the United Church. That was a very legitimate concern, and we put it in an amendment.
I assume that the hon. member for York-Peel and other Conservatives who are so critical of banks will vote against our amendment, even though they should not.
November 19, 1980

The hon. member for York-Peel criticized the government for permitting and encouraging foreign banks to come to Canada. This party does not believe they should be coming, and that is part of the reason we will vote against the bill. After listening to the long speech of the hon. member, 1 assume he will vote for the bill. So much for his opposition to foreign banks.
We are opposed to foreign banks. This government failed significantly to expand the powers of the near banks and so the foreign banks will carry the ball for the government's argument for increased competition. We believe it would have been healthy and more consistent with a policy of gaining control of the Canadian economy, to strengthen Canadian financial institutions rather than encouraging more subsidiaries of foreign banks. We think that foreign banks will concentrate on wholesale or large scale commercial business. Statistics from the Bank of Canada support this view. Assets of the 35 to 40 foreign banks operating in Canada through their representatives' offices have grown by 169 per cent over the last four years-from $1.7 billion in 1975 to $4.8 billion this year, while the assets of the Canadian chartered banks have increased by just 94 per cent.
That is the case with the foreign banks, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for York-Peel made quite a critique of them and then, with his Conservative colleagues, proposes to vote for this Bank Act which will permit them to expand.
We heard the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte complain that the banks do not look after the interests of small business. In the committee, our members proposed amendments that would require the banks to allocate more of the capital they have available for loans to small business, but the Conservatives voted against that suggestion. We argued that banks should direct their funds to more useful purposes. We proposed that they should be required to make more of their investment portfolios available for housing at a reasonable rate of interest, especially housing for low and moderate income people. Of course this was not supported by the Conservative party. They are not prepared to put their votes where their mouths are.
The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte argued that the banks do not make money available for loans to farmers or fishermen in the small towns and rural areas. When we proposed amendments which would require them to do just that, the Conservatives voted with the government against them.
We heard the hon. member for Calgary North complain about the amendments that our members of the finance committee proposed to this bill. Of course they proposed an amendment which we felt would strengthen the Bank Act and which would have directed the banks to make part of their portfolios available to people in isolated and rural areas. Some Conservative members had been calling for it, but when it came to the vote they were conspicuous by their absence. They certainly did not propose such an amendment themselves.
The hon. member seemed worried about the possible nationalization of the banks but, Mr. Speaker, no member of this House argued for that. There is nothing in this bill which

would indicate movement in that direction. I suppose what he was talking about was the fear that the government is going to take over the oil industry. Mr. Speaker, there are many people who, like president-elect of the United States, Ronald Reagan, are opposed to public ownership. We could discuss the merits of American public ownership and of private ownership. I am puzzled and confused when I hear members of the Conservative party argue against public ownership.
There are publicly-owned telephone companies in western Canada, Mr. Speaker. In 1908 a Conservative government in Manitoba established a publicly-owned telephone company, and no one since then has suggested they should get rid of it. Alberta also has a publicly-owned telephone system. That province has had a Conservative government for a number of years and before that it had a Conservative government which called itself a Social Credit government. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) could tell us about it. It never moved to get rid of the publicly-owned telephone system. Almost every province has a publicly-owned power company and many of these were started by Conservative governments and expanded by Conservative governments. No one has suggested we should get rid of that public ownership.
The Conservative government of Alberta has taken over Pacific Western Airlines which is now a wholly-owned public corporation. I do not know how they can square that with their belief in free enterprise. Then there is the Alberta Energy Company, Nova Corporation, the Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company. All of these have a substantial public investment, and they were established by the Conservative government of Alberta.
I have to assume that the Conservatives oppose public ownership except when it is proposed by Conservative governments. That is a very interesting way of looking at things.

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the companies the hon. member has just mentioned are in competition. They do not have a monopoly; they are in competition with others, and the shares are owned by the public.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my understanding that the Alberta telephone system is in competition with any other, but it may be. Petro-Canada is certainly in competition with the privately-owned energy corporations. Even this party has not suggested that all energy corporations should be taken over and run by the state.
I would remind the hon. member for Bow River that in almost every other country in the world, whether Norway, Sweden or any western European country, governments own a very substantial percentage of most of the new oil and gas development in recent years. Since World War I, BP has been 50 per cent publicly owned. That great exponent of socialism, Winston Churchill, took over 50 per cent of it.
I should like to take a few moments to indicate some of our reservations about this bill, Mr. Speaker, and why we propose to vote against it. We not only speak against the bill, we vote against it. That illustrates the difference between this party

November 19, 1980
Bank Act
and the Conservative party which speaks against the bill and then will vote for it, as I believe it will.
We are against this bill because, in our opinion, it fails to meet the needs of the Canadian people. We believe that for too long the Canadian banking system has been allowed a central position in the economy of this country without playing a key role for the benefit of Canadian citizens. That is not to suggest that the banks have necessarily abused their position. What I am saying is that the opportunity to use the banking system as an instrument of public policy to benefit Canadians, and to strengthen our economy, has been missed and it will continue to be missed if we pass this bill as it has been drafted.
The disparities and the weaknesses of the Canadian economy are well known and well documented. What is especially worrying to us is that these disparities and weaknesses result from underlying trends in the national economy which continue to go untreated. The problem of regional disparity is getting worse, and is accompanied by very high unemployment. In fact we have the highest rate of unemployment in the industrialized world. We also have low rates of job creation. The manufacturing sector in this country is deteriorating. The share of that sector in the national work force is dropping. It has dropped from 26 per cent in 1973 to 19 per cent in 1979. Research and development are inadequately funded. In the past five years, $13.8 billion in dividends and interest payments has left the country. A further $8.5 billion left in management fees, patent fees, licence fees, copyright fees and the like.
We say the banks are, to a large extent, responsible for that situation because the banks have not been directed by governments of this country, Liberal or Conservative, to play a socially useful function in this economy of ours. We say the banks should be one of the best instruments for helping to put this country back to work by developing resources for the benefit of Canadians. Instead, the banks have been given tremendous economic power. They have used it largely to benefit their directors and shareholders.
I do not want to repeat today some of the things I have said on other occasions, and which other members of our party have said. However, the system of interlocking directorships we have in Canada in which bank directors are also directors of other corporations, has helped to build a resource not just at the banks, which have grown at a tremendous rate, but has helped to give an even greater stranglehold each year to the large corporations in Canada.
We have a situation where directors of each of the major banks are in turn directors of the major industrial and business corporations in Canada. The Royal Bank of Canada, the Bank of Montreal, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, in fact all of them are involved in this kind of operation. Directors of the large corporations, such as the president of the CPR, the president of Seagram's, the president of Brascan, and other corporations are in turn directors of banks. Each of them is interested in seeing their corporations grow. They grow obviously at the expense of the small businessman, the local
entrepreneur, for whom our friends in the Conservative party have so often expressed sympathy, and on whose behalf they are very loath to do anything of any real significance to help.
We do not apologize for our opposition to this bill, nor do we apologize that our members did what the hon. member for Calgary North said they did, and that was bring in a large number of amendments. They did it knowingly and with the support of all members of our party. They did it because we have fundamental disagreements with the government and with Conservative members of Parliament who, despite all of their protestations, are going to vote for this bill. They will vote for this bill despite being so critical of so many of the provisions in it, because they wrote the bill. The former minister of finance helped draft this bill, as did the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). And to whom did these people go for help? They went to the very people this bill is supposed to regulate and monitor, the people in the banking community. They got the kind of bill, despite the protestations of some of their backbenchers, which the bankers wanted.
The same bill which was introduced by the former minister of finance, with very few amendments or changes, comes back today in this session brought forward by a Liberal government. It proves again what we have said so often, that there is virtually no difference between the Liberal and Conservative parties.
I conclude by saying that we are going to vote against this bill despite the claims of the hon. member for York-Peel that there is a coalition between the Liberals and the NDP. I am certain that members of the Conservative party are going to vote for the bill. These votes we will have will demonstrate very clearly to Canadians that if there is a coalition of parties in this Parliament, it is between the two old line parties, the Liberals and the Conservatives. We, as always, oppose this bill and bills like it which are brought forward either by Conservative or Liberal governments.
